articles.full_text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC) - This week’s heat wave will continue through today. Temperatures will soar into the mid-to-upper 90s this afternoon. High humidity levels may make it feel as hot as 110°. (Oddly enough, today is the first day that the “normal” or “average” high drops to 89° in Charleston.)
The National Weather Service has issued yet another Heat Advisory for the coastal corridor today. Georgetown, Charleston, tidal Berkeley, coastal Colleton, and Beaufort counties will be under a Heat Advisory from 11:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.
Inland, heat index values will still exceed 100° this afternoon.
With the heat and humidity of the day, and a stationary front draped west of the Lowcountry, scattered showers and storms will be likely this afternoon. At this time, it appears that the greatest coverage of storms (and therefore, the greatest impacts) will be inland.
Some storms may be strong-to-severe and capable of producing damaging winds, frequent lightning, and heavy rain. Storms will be moving slowly and may move repeatedly over the same areas, exacerbating the risk of localized flooding.
Lingering showers and thunderstorms are possible overnight Friday into Saturday morning.
Additional, occasional showers and storms will be possible throughout the day on Saturday. Sunday will be the driest day of the weekend with only isolated showers and storms in the area.
Temperatures will finally be a little more tolerable this weekend. The Live 5 First Alert Weather team is forecasting highs in the low 90s on Saturday. Highs may reach the mid 90s on Sunday, but humidity levels should be noticeably lower during the second half of the weekend.
Click here to download the free Live 5 First Alert Weather app for the latest weather information.
TROPICS: The tropical Atlantic, Gulf, and Caribbean remain fairly quiet at this time.
As of Friday morning, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) is watching a weak area of low pressure in the central subtropical Atlantic. This system is a few hundred miles east-southeast of Bermuda. It will likely drift west-southwestward through Sunday before making a turn northward and out to sea early next week. The NHC is giving this disturbance a low chance (10%) of formation through the next 48 hours and a low chance (20%) of formation through the next seven days.
The NHC is also monitoring a non-tropical area of low pressure over the northeastern Atlantic, well off the coast of Portugal. This system may acquire some subtropical or tropical characteristics this weekend as it moves east southeastward at 10 - 15 mph toward Portugal and northwestern Spain. The NHC is giving this system a low chance (20%) of formation through the next 48 hours and a low chance (20%) of formation through the next seven days.
By the end of this month, and into the first week of September, long-range forecast models have hinted at a gradual increase in activity in the central and eastern tropical Atlantic. The team will continue to monitor trends over the coming days.
